newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole vie for Mideast diplomatic spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole vie for Mideast diplomatic spotlight.

text.p: Political rivals Bob Dole and President Bill Clinton vied for the diplomatic spotlight surrounding Tuesday's Middle East summit, as a federal court ruling kept Ross Perot out of the presidential debates.

While Clinton hosted Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Jordan's King Hussein at the White House for emergency talks to restart the regional peace process, Republican Dole took aim at the Democrat's "photo op foreign policy."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry dismissed Dole's critique as not worthy of comment. "I can understand his frustation and wanting to try to make some news today, but I'll leave aside his comments and try to stay focused on the work the president's doing."

But the photo opportunities abounded, with Clinton and the three Middle East leaders seen in televised pictures strolling around the White House grounds. Clinton stayed in camera range but largely out of earshot, leaving it to Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota to strike back at Dole.
Daschle told reporters Dole was close to "crossing the line in a very, very sensitive area of international involvement for the country today."

Dole's national campaign chairman, Donald Rumsfeld, said the former Kansas senator was well within the bounds of propriety in commenting on Clinton's foreign policy, telling CNN that such discussions could not be put "on hold ... for weeks on end simply because various events intervene."

Campaigning in the Midwest, Dole also targeted Clinton's debating abilities, warning an adoring crowd in Kirtland, Ohio, not to believe what the president would say in televised debates set to begin on Sunday.
"When you are listening to the debates, ask yourself this question: 'Would you buy a used campaign promise from this man?'" Dole asked supporters in his first campaign appearance in three days.
Reform Party presidential candidate Perot got bad news from a federal judge in Washington, who ruled against Perot's attempt to be included in presidential debates.
Perot sought to reverse a decision by the bipartisan Commission on Presidential Debates. His attorneys said they would appeal the ruling.
With five weeks to go before the November 5 general election, Dole was working hard to shore up support in the heartland states that have traditionally been kind to Republicans.

The latest polls showed Dole trailing Clinton by a double-digit margin. A new Reuters tracking poll put the president ahead by 11 percentage points, with 44.9 percent to Dole's 33.8 percent and Perot's 5 percent. 14.4 percent of respondents were undecided.

A Harris Poll gave Clinton a 21-point lead, with 55 percent compared with Dole's 34 percent and Perot's 7 percent. A CNN/USA Today Gallup tracking poll put the gap at 25 points, giving Clinton 57 percent, Dole 32 percent and Perot 5 percent, but Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart discounted this as overly optimistic.
Internal White House polls have put Clinton's lead in the mid-teens.
